claim: AWS WAF evaluates the rules of a web ACL or rule group from the lowest numeric priority setting upward until it finds a match that terminates the evaluation or runs out of rules.
question: In which order does AWS WAF evaluate the rules of a web ACL, and when does it stop?

values.display: from the lowest numeric priority setting on up
finds a match that terminates the evaluation

qualifiers.scope: per web ACL or rule group

evidence.quote: When AWS WAF evaluates any rule group, protection pack (web ACL) against a web request, it evaluates the rules from the lowest numeric priority setting on up until it either finds a match that terminates the evaluation or exhausts all of the rules.

claim: Each rule in a web ACL must have a unique priority setting within that web ACL, and each rule in a rule group a unique priority within that rule group.
question: Can two rules in one web ACL share the same priority?

values.display: a unique priority setting
using numeric priority settings

qualifiers.scope: per web ACL or rule group

evidence.quote: You must give each rule in a protection pack (web ACL) a unique priority setting within that protection pack (web ACL), and you must give each rule in a rule group a unique priority setting within that rule group.

claim: You must set a default action on every web ACL; AWS WAF applies it to any request that passes all rule evaluations without a terminating action being applied.
question: What happens to a request that no rule in the web ACL terminates?

values.display: you must set the protection pack (web ACL) default action
without having a terminating action applied to it

evidence.quote: When you create and configure a protection pack (web ACL), you must set the protection pack (web ACL) default action. AWS WAF applies this action to any web request that makes it through all of the protection pack (web ACL)'s rule evaluations without having a terminating action applied to it.

claim: The web ACL default action must decide the final disposition of the request, so it is a terminating action: Allow or Block.
question: Which actions can be the default action of a web ACL?

values.display: so it's a terminating action
must determine the final disposition

evidence.quote: The protection pack (web ACL) default action must determine the final disposition of the web request, so it's a terminating action:

claim: Rule actions are terminating or non-terminating; a terminating action stops the web ACL evaluation of the request and either lets it continue to the protected application or blocks it.
question: What does a terminating rule action do?

values.display: stops the protection pack (web ACL) evaluation
terminating or non-terminating

evidence.quote: Rule actions can be terminating or non-terminating. A terminating action stops the protection pack (web ACL) evaluation of the request and either lets it continue to your protected application or blocks it.

claim: Count is a non-terminating action: AWS WAF counts the request and continues processing the remaining rules in the web ACL; in your own rules, Count can insert custom headers and add labels that other rules can match.
question: After a rule with the Count action matches, does AWS WAF keep evaluating the other rules?

values.display: This is a non-terminating action.
AWS WAF continues processing the remaining rules
add labels that other rules can match against

evidence.quote: This is a non-terminating action. AWS WAF continues processing the remaining rules in the protection pack (web ACL). In rules that you define, you can insert custom headers into the request and you can add labels that other rules can match against.

claim: When AWS WAF blocks a request, by default the protected AWS resource responds with an HTTP 403 (Forbidden) status code; in rules you define, you can customize the response.
question: What does a client receive by default when AWS WAF blocks its request?

values.display: HTTP `403 (Forbidden)` status code
you can customize the response

qualifiers.condition: custom response configured in the rule or default action

evidence.quote: By default, your protected AWS resource responds with an HTTP `403 (Forbidden)` status code. In rules that you define, you can customize the response.

claim: With the Allow action, in rules that you define, AWS WAF can insert custom headers into the request before forwarding it to the protected resource.
question: Can AWS WAF add a header to a request it allows, for the origin to read?

evidence.quote: In rules that you define, you can insert custom headers into the request before forwarding it to the protected resource.

claim: CAPTCHA puzzles and silent challenges can run only when browsers access HTTPS endpoints, and browser clients must run in secure contexts to get tokens.
question: Can the CAPTCHA or Challenge action work for an HTTP-only endpoint?

values.display: can only run when browsers are accessing HTTPS endpoints
must be running in secure contexts

evidence.quote: CAPTCHA puzzles and silent challenges can only run when browsers are accessing HTTPS endpoints. Browser clients must be running in secure contexts in order to acquire tokens.

claim: You are charged additional fees when you use the CAPTCHA or Challenge rule action in a rule or as a rule action override in a rule group.
question: Does using the CAPTCHA or Challenge action cost extra?

values.display: You are charged additional fees

evidence.quote: You are charged additional fees when you use the CAPTCHA or Challenge rule action in one of your rules or as a rule action override in a rule group.

claim: For a request with a valid, unexpired token (by the configured immunity time), the CAPTCHA and Challenge actions behave like Count and AWS WAF continues inspecting the remaining rules.
question: What does a CAPTCHA or Challenge rule do with a request that carries a valid token?

values.display: similar to the Count action
If the token is valid and unexpired

qualifiers.condition: token valid and within the immunity time

evidence.quote: AWS WAF continues to inspect the web request based on the remaining rules in the protection pack (web ACL).
If the token is valid and unexpired according to the configured CAPTCHA or challenge immunity time, AWS WAF handles the request similar to the Count action.

claim: For a request whose token is invalid or expired, AWS WAF terminates inspection and blocks the request (like Block), then responds with a custom response code: a CAPTCHA puzzle for CAPTCHA, or a silent challenge in a JavaScript interstitial for Challenge.
question: What does a CAPTCHA or Challenge rule do with a request that has no valid token?

values.display: terminates the inspection of the web request and blocks the request
sends a CAPTCHA puzzle in a JavaScript interstitial
a JavaScript interstitial with a silent challenge

evidence.quote: If the token is invalid or the indicated timestamp is expired, AWS WAF terminates the inspection of the web request and blocks the request, similar to the Block action.

For CAPTCHA, if the request contents indicate that the client browser can handle it, AWS WAF sends a CAPTCHA puzzle in a JavaScript interstitial, which is designed to distinguish human clients from bots.
For the Challenge action, AWS WAF sends a JavaScript interstitial with a silent challenge that is designed to distinguish normal browsers from sessions that are being run by bots.

claim: Managed rule group rules usually use the Block action, but not all do; for example, some Bot Control rules use the CAPTCHA and Challenge actions.
question: Do all managed rule group rules block matching requests?

values.display: usually use the Block action, but not all do

evidence.quote: Managed rule group rules usually use the Block action, but not all do. For examples, some rules used for Bot Control use the CAPTCHA and Challenge action settings.
